title: Doubt
hook: Thomas doubted and was met, not rejected
tomorrow: what if you pray and feel nothing at all, for months?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two fires and three questions: Peter failed, and was trusted again. Today, the apostle who wouldn't take anyone's word for it.

Pics or it didn't happen. Every group chat has the friend who wants proof, and the friend who rolls their eyes at them. Thomas was the proof friend. The other apostles tell him they've seen Jesus alive, and he won't take their word for it. People have nicknamed him Doubting Thomas. So was he wrong? Inside the Church, the question has two sides, and each one has a real case.
screen: `PICS OR IT DIDN'T HAPPEN.` → `THOMAS WANTS PROOF.` → `WAS HE WRONG?`

segments.voice: Thomas wasn't there when Jesus came. So he sets terms: unless he sees the nail marks and puts his hand in the wound, he won't believe. When Jesus comes back, he doesn't send Thomas away. He offers the wounds, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "put it into my side; and be not faithless, but believing." Thomas answers, "My Lord, and my God." One side says: faith is a gift you guard. Jesus adds, "blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed." The Catechism calls willful doubt, refusing to hold what God has revealed, a sin against faith. On this view, doubt isn't a hobby. It's a crack to tend before it spreads. The other side says: doubt can be part of the road. The same Catechism names a different thing, involuntary doubt, the hesitation of someone struggling with objections, and doesn't treat it the same way. In Mark's Gospel, a father cries out, "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief," and Jesus heals his son anyway. Here's one to tell a friend: John Henry Newman, an English convert later named a saint, wrote that "ten thousand difficulties do not make one doubt." Hard questions aren't the same as walking away. Both sides keep one thing: Thomas brought his doubt into the room, and it was met.
screen: `BE NOT FAITHLESS, BUT BELIEVING.` · `ONE SIDE: GUARD THE GIFT.` · `THE OTHER: HELP MY UNBELIEF.` · `DIFFICULTIES AREN'T DOUBT.` · then, large: `DOUBT WAS MET.`

segments.voice: Sit with your hands open on your knees, palms up. Bring one real doubt, and set it in your hands instead of hiding it. If you pray, you can say the father's line, I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief, and keep your hands open while the sit runs.
Doubt. Not being sure. In John, the doubter's question gets an answer, not a closed door.
Keep this: doubt was met, because Thomas asked to touch and Jesus held out his hands. Good night.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Thomas's story every year on the Second Sunday of Easter, and some say his words, my Lord and my God, silently when the host is raised at Mass.

chat.says: Abuela's friend Doña Carmen got bad news. i prayed but i'm not sure anyone's listening. does that count?
options: It counts. 'I do believe, help my unbelief' is a prayer right in the Gospel.
Not really. Doubt cancels prayer out, so wait until you're sure, then pray.
Doubt is just a sin, so confess it first and hold off praying till then.
chat.meaning: The father in Mark prayed with his doubt, and Thomas brought his into the room. In both stories, the doubt was met.

CCC 2088 paraphrased: voluntary doubt disregards or refuses to hold as true what God has revealed (a sin against faith); involuntary doubt refers to hesitation in believing, difficulty in overcoming objections. Confirm the paraphrase and that 'doesn't treat it the same way' is fair.

Newman, Apologia ch. 5: 'Ten thousand difficulties do not make one doubt, as I understand the subject'. The number is in the cited text. Newman: convert (1845), cardinal, canonized (2019); the voice says only 'an English convert later named a saint'. Confirm.
Debate day: both views are Catholic and presented without a verdict; the shared point (the doubt was met) is from John 20.
